subject: physics
title: Distance, speed and time
overview: Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total elapsed time.
workedExample: A vehicle covering 120 km in 3 h has an average speed of 40 km/h.
limitation: Distinguish average speed from instantaneous speed and displacement from distance.

subject: physics
title: Acceleration
overview: Acceleration measures the rate at which velocity changes over time.
workedExample: If velocity changes from 2 to 10 m/s in 4 s, average acceleration is 2 m/s².
limitation: The formula assumes the stated time interval and a consistent sign convention.

subject: physics
title: Newton's second law
overview: For constant mass in an inertial frame, net force equals mass multiplied by acceleration.
workedExample: A net force of 6 N on a mass of 2 kg gives acceleration 3 m/s².
limitation: This uses net force, not an arbitrary single force when other forces act.

subject: physics
title: Density
overview: Density is mass per unit volume for the stated material and conditions.
workedExample: A sample of mass 120 g and volume 40 cm³ has density 3 g/cm³.
limitation: Temperature, phase and porosity affect how density should be interpreted.

subject: physics
title: Pressure
overview: For a uniform perpendicular force distributed over area, pressure equals force divided by that area.
workedExample: A 200 N force spread uniformly over 0.5 m² gives 400 Pa.
limitation: Use the perpendicular component of force; fluid pressure also depends on depth.

subject: physics
title: Ohm's law
overview: For an ohmic conductor at constant conditions, potential difference is the product of current and resistance.
workedExample: A 12 V source across a 4 Ω ideal resistor produces 3 A.
limitation: Real components may be non-ohmic or change resistance as they heat.

subject: physics
title: Electrical power
overview: Instantaneous electrical power delivered to a device is potential difference multiplied by current.
workedExample: At 6 V and 2 A, power is 12 W.
limitation: This does not by itself establish electrical safety or real device efficiency.

subject: physics
title: Wave speed
overview: For a periodic wave in a defined medium, speed equals frequency times wavelength.
workedExample: A 100 Hz wave with wavelength 3 m travels at 300 m/s in that medium.
limitation: Wave speed depends on the physical medium and type of wave.

subject: physics
title: Thin-lens equation
overview: For a paraxial thin lens using a consistent sign convention, focal length relates object and image distances.
workedExample: For a convex lens with f = 10 cm and real object at u = 30 cm, the real image is at v = 15 cm.
limitation: The example assumes the positive-real-distance convention for a converging lens.

subject: physics
title: Simple pendulum period
overview: For small angles and negligible drag, a simple pendulum's period depends on length and gravitational acceleration.
workedExample: For L = 1 m and g ≈ 9.81 m/s², period is approximately 2.01 s.
limitation: The small-angle model does not remain exact for large amplitudes.

subject: physics
title: Kinetic energy
overview: Translational kinetic energy in a nonrelativistic frame depends on mass and squared speed.
workedExample: For m = 2 kg and v = 3 m/s, kinetic energy is 9 J.
limitation: The velocity must be defined relative to a chosen frame.

subject: biology
title: Onion epidermal cells
overview: A thin onion epidermis can be prepared for light microscopy to observe regular plant cell boundaries.
observation: Look for a cell wall and often a large vacuole; a typical onion bulb epidermis has no chloroplasts.
limitation: Handle sharp preparation tools and stains with teacher supervision.

subject: biology
title: Human cheek cells
overview: Cheek epithelial cells illustrate animal cell boundaries and nuclei in a suitable stained smear.
observation: Unlike plant cells, animal cells lack a rigid cellulose cell wall.
limitation: Any specimen involving people requires consent, hygienic disposal and school policy.

subject: biology
title: Paramecium
overview: Paramecium is a single-celled ciliate often studied for movement and cell organisation.
observation: Observe ciliary movement and distinguish its whole organism from a multicellular tissue.
limitation: Do not collect unknown contaminated water or handle cultures without supervision.

subject: biology
title: Euglena
overview: Euglena includes flagellated protists with diverse nutrition; some species have chloroplasts.
observation: Compare locomotion and chloroplast-bearing cells without assuming all species are identical.
limitation: Observe prepared material; identify organisms carefully rather than guessing from shape alone.

subject: biology
title: Amoeba
overview: Amoeboid protists illustrate flexible cell shapes, cytoplasmic streaming and pseudopodia.
observation: Watch how a cell changes outline while moving or feeding.
limitation: Amoeba is a broad instructional label; species identification requires evidence.

subject: biology
title: Baker's yeast
overview: Yeast is a single-celled fungus often used to demonstrate budding and fermentation.
observation: Observe budding under suitable magnification and compare with bacterial binary fission.
limitation: Use food-safe classroom samples under teacher instruction, not unknown cultures.

subject: biology
title: Spirogyra
overview: Spirogyra consists of filamentous green algae known for spiral chloroplast arrangements.
observation: Recognise that a filament comprises individual cells joined end to end.
limitation: Avoid treating all green filaments as Spirogyra without microscopic features.

subject: biology
title: Leaf stomata
overview: Stomata are epidermal pores controlled by guard cells and participate in gas exchange.
observation: A leaf surface preparation can show the pores and surrounding guard cells.
limitation: Pore state varies with plant species, environmental conditions and handling.

subject: biology
title: Root hairs
overview: Root hairs are extensions of some epidermal cells that increase contact with soil water and nutrients.
observation: Compare surface area and distinguish the root hair from a separate multicellular organ.
limitation: Water uptake pathways depend on living tissue and surrounding conditions.

subject: biology
title: Blood components
overview: Blood contains plasma and formed elements such as red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
observation: Compare schematic sizes and roles, not a clinical diagnosis from a simulation.
limitation: Never collect blood in an unsupervised classroom; use vetted prepared slides.

subject: agriculture
title: Maize
overview: A cereal crop commonly studied for its roots, stem, leaves, tassel and ear.
observation: Distinguish germination, vegetative growth, flowering and grain development.
limitation: Growth and fertiliser needs vary by variety, soil, season and local conditions.

subject: agriculture
title: Rice
overview: An important cereal with panicles bearing grains; cultivation systems include upland and flooded lowland fields.
observation: Compare soil-water management concepts between different rice production systems.
limitation: Standing water needs and pest pressures vary; classroom notes are not field prescriptions.

subject: agriculture
title: Sorghum
overview: A cereal with a characteristic grain-bearing panicle, studied across dryland farming systems.
observation: Compare crop traits and the concept of adaptation to water availability.
limitation: Tolerance differs across varieties and growth stages; drought does not guarantee good yield.

subject: agriculture
title: Pearl millet
overview: A cereal grown in many semi-arid environments, useful when discussing adaptation and crop diversity.
observation: Identify the seed, leaves and inflorescence and compare with maize and sorghum.
limitation: Production advice must come from local extension guidance and verified field conditions.

subject: agriculture
title: Cassava
overview: A tropical crop cultivated for starchy storage roots and often propagated using stem cuttings.
observation: Explain the difference between vegetative propagation and seed germination.
limitation: Unprocessed cassava may contain cyanogenic compounds; food processing safety is essential.

subject: agriculture
title: Cowpea
overview: A grain legume used to study roots, flowers, pods and relationships with nitrogen-fixing symbionts.
observation: Describe the general idea of symbiotic nitrogen fixation and crop rotations.
limitation: Not all soils or plants nodulate effectively; a field test requires local evidence.

subject: agriculture
title: Groundnut / peanut
overview: A legume with pods that develop underground, useful for classifying reproductive structures.
observation: Compare above-ground flowers with subterranean pod development.
limitation: Poor drying and storage can increase fungal contamination risk; follow food safety rules.

subject: agriculture
title: Tomato
overview: A fruiting crop used to explain pollination, fruit development and plant water transport.
observation: Relate flower and fruit structures to soil water and nutrient availability.
limitation: Similar leaf symptoms have multiple causes; do not diagnose deficiencies from photographs alone.

subject: agriculture
title: Domestic cattle
overview: Large ruminants used to introduce digestion, nutrition, housing and animal welfare.
observation: Compare ruminant digestive adaptations with monogastric animals.
limitation: Animal illness requires a qualified veterinary professional.

subject: agriculture
title: Domestic goat
overview: Small ruminants used to discuss feeding behaviour, housing and responsible livestock management.
observation: Compare browsing behaviour and basic welfare requirements with other livestock.
limitation: Do not substitute a classroom profile for professional husbandry or veterinary advice.

subject: agriculture
title: Domestic chicken
overview: Poultry used to study egg development, feeding and flock health.
observation: Identify basic external features and explain why clean drinking water matters.
limitation: Disease, vaccines and feed formulation require reliable local veterinary guidance.
